heading: Blood Culture
html:
• Volume of blood collected is most critical
  • Disinfect the venipuncture site
  • Catheter-drawn blood cultures have a higher risk of contamination
  • Do not submit catheter tips for culture without an accompanying blood culture obtained by venipuncture

heading: CNS Infection
html:
• Meningitis, encephalitis, focal infections of brain parenchyma, CNS shunt infections, subdural empyema, epidural abscess
  • Routes of infection: hematogenous spread, direct spread from an infected site, anatomic defects in CNS structures, nerves
  • Ix: culture, molecular (viral – enterovirus, herpesvirus), Ag detection (fungal – cryptococcus)
  • Blood cultures should be obtained if meningitis is suspected
  • Inform the microbiology laboratory if unusual organisms are suspected
  • Collect 3-4 tubes of CSF by lumbar puncture and submit for bacterial culture and molecular testing
  • Collect as much sample as possible

heading: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections (SSTIs)
html:
• Primary cutaneous infections: cellulitis, ecthyma, impetigo, folliculitis, furunculosis, erysipelas
  • Do not use the label “wound” alone
  • The specimen of choice is a biopsied sample of the advancing margin of the lesion
  • Do not ask the laboratory to report everything that grows

heading: Antimicrobial Susceptibility
html:
• Susceptibility testing: used to produce antimicrobial susceptibility profiles and detect resistance to therapeutic agents
  • Standardization: optimizes bacterial growth, optimizes conditions, maintains reproducibility
  • Breakpoint: minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) or zone diameter value used to categorize S, SDD, I, R, NS
  • Interpretive category: derived from microbiological characteristic, PK-PD parameters, and clinical outcome data

heading: Clostridial Species
html:
• Gram-positive bacilli, anaerobic, spore forming, +/– toxin-producing
  • Spore: a unit of sexual or asexual reproduction that may be adapted for dispersal and for survival, often for extended periods of time, in unfavourable conditions; metabolically inactive; hard to destroy
  • Ix: nucleic acid amplification test (C. difficile toxin gene), ELISA (C. difficile common antigen, C. difficile toxin); difficult to culture
Clostridial SpeciesDiseases Caused
Clostridium difficileDiarrhea; pseudomembranous colitis
Large clostridial toxins TcdA and TcdB: enter epithelial cells to cause inflammatory cytokine (IL1-β) and chemokine production, influx of
neutrophils, disruption of tight junctions, fluid secretion, and cell death (TcdB is most potent)
CDTb binds to epithelial receptor and is endocytosed; CDTb oligomerizes and forms a pore
CDTa is translocated through the pore and enters the cytoplasm as the endosome acidifies (vacuolar ATPase); CDTa ribosylates actin,
leading to complete destruction of the cellular actin cytoskeleton, loss of cell shape and tight junctions, and cell death
Clostridium perfringensGangrene: blood flow to a large area of tissue is cut off, causing the tissue to break down and die (greenish-black color)
Clostridium tetaniTetanus – trismus (lock jaw), risus sardonicus (Sardinian grin), opisthotonos (backward arching)
Inhibits the release of GABA/glycine; uncontrolled release of neurotransmitter = muscle contractions/spasms
Clostridium botulinumInfant botulism (flaccid paralysis) – gut colonisation, honey contaminated by spores, environmental dust/soil containing spores
Foodborne botulism – self-canned products, prison brew (pruno, hooch, moonshine, bootleg)
Wound botulism
Iatrogenic botulism
Inhibits acetylcholine release = no muscle contraction

heading: Body Temperature
html:
• Thermal compartments: core = internal organs and muscles; shell = skin and subcutaneous fat
  • o Fluctuations of temperature in the peripheral regions help maintain the core body temperature
  • Normal oral temperature = 37 ° C (35.5-37.7 ° C) – no single temperature can be used as the upper limit of normal
  • Physiological variations: circadian rhythm (peak temperature = 2 PM; lowest temperature = 4 AM), menstrual cycle, post- menopausal hot flashes and fever
  • The homeostatic control of body temperature (regulated variable) involves a negative feedback system composed of sensors, an integrating center, and effectors
  • o Thermoreceptors: sensor neurons that are activated by warmth or cold – skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, brain
  • o Hypothalamus integrates the input from thermoreceptors – anterior = heat (front, fire), posterior = cold (back, brrr)
  • Feedforward mechanism: the body acts in anticipation of thermal changes
  • 1 ° C increase in body temperature = 4.4 bpm increase in HR
  • Thermoregulation reaches adult levels once puberty ends – girls = 13-14 years; boys = 17-18 years

heading: Fever
html:
• Fever: a state of elevated core body temperature that is often, but not necessarily, part of the host defense against invasion by microorganisms or inanimate matter recognized as pathogenic or foreign
  • Early morning (6 AM) oral/tympanic temperature ≥ 37.2 ° C (99.0 ° F); any oral/tympanic temperature ≥ 37.8 ° C (100 ° F)
  • Fever inhibits the growth of many microorganisms, increases the production of antibodies, and stimulates the innate and adaptive immune responses to infections
  • Common symptoms: rise in body temperature (with subsequent sweating and falling of body temperature), chills, rigors
  • Variable symptoms: headache, malaise, anorexia
  • Fever of unknown origin: temperature ≥ 101 ° F documented clinically on several separate occasions, where an appropriate initial diagnostic workup does not reveal etiology of fever

heading: Transmission of Microorganisms and Chain of Infection
html:
• Not all exposures lead to transmission and infection
  • The probability of transmission and infection is dependent on host susceptibility, microorganism inoculum size, viability and virulence, and the effectiveness of control measures
  • Herd immunity: when a high enough proportion of individuals in a population are resistant to an agent, then those few who are susceptible will be protected by the resistant majority, since the pathogen will be unlikely to “find” the susceptible individuals
  • Aerosol-generating medical procedures: intubation, manual ventilation, open endotracheal suctioning, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, bronchoscopy, sputum induction nebulized therapy, autopsy, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP)

heading: Choosing an Antimicrobial Agent
html:
• Must know the identity (or likely identity) of the infecting organism on the basis of clinical information
  • Information about the susceptibility (or likely susceptibility) of the infecting organisms must be as accurate as possible
  • Host factors: drug allergies, site of infection, pregnancy, regional susceptibility information, renal/hepatic function (eGFR), recent antibiotic exposure, community vs. hospital infection, DDIs; comorbidities, immunocompromised, older age
  • Drug factors: safety record, success record, microbial etiology, bactericidal/bacteriostatic, penetration into site, adverse effects
  • Direct adverse effects: neutropenia/thrombocytopenia/nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity/neurotoxicity, DDIs, allergic reactions
  • Indirect adverse effects: effects on normal bowel flora, increased risk of infection with drug-resistant pathogens

Cell wall
synthesis		𝛃 -lactams
-Most commonly prescribed class of antimicrobial agents; used for the treatment of a wide variety of infections
-Relatively safe therapeutic index – safest group of antibiotics in pregnant patients
-Low concentrations in the eyes and CSF/brain (penetrates BBB with meningeal inflammation)
-Therapeutic concentrations in lungs, liver, kidneys urine, prostate, and bone
-Inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, which normally catalyze the linking peptidoglycan – bactericidal
-Increasing resistance with overuse – 𝛃 -lactamases (hydrolyze the 𝛽 -lactam ring and render the antibiotic inactive before it reaches the
peptidoglycan target site); target penicillin-binding protein modifications

(no S. aureus coverage)		Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G), phenoxypenicillins (penicillin V), aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin), isoxazolyl
penicillins (anti-staphylococcal – cloxacillin)

(no enterococcus
coverage)		1 st generation (cefazolin, cephalexin/Keflex)Gram-positive cocci activity; limited gram-negative bacilli activity
2 nd generation (cefuroxime)Improved gram-negative activity
Some agents have activity against anaerobes – cefoxitin, cefotetan
3 rd generation (ceftriaxone)Variable gram-positive activity; improved gram-negative activity
4 th generationEfficacy against most clinical gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria
5 th generationEnhanced activity against MRSA and gram-negative bacilli
Anti-pseudomonal (ceftazidime)
CarbapenemsImipenem, meropenem, ertapenem
-Broadest spectrum of activity of all antibiotics
-Active against gram-positives, gram-negatives, and anaerobes
-Do not cover some drug-resistant organisms – methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), vancomycin-resistant
enterococci (VRE), carbapenem-resistant organisms (CRO)
- Should be reserved for serious, life-threatening infections or those caused by multi-drug resistant organisms
MonobactamsAztreonam (not used in Canada)
Glycopeptides
Vancomycin- Weakly bactericidal agent that binds directly to the peptidoglycan bacterial cell wall, inhibiting cross-linking – leaky
-Effective against most gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA
-Uses: cardiovascular, bone and joint, skin and soft-tissue, intraabdominal, and CNS infections; C. difficile oral therapy
-Nephrotoxic
Nucleic
acid
synthesis		Fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase)
-Synthetic antimicrobial agents that inhibit the ligase activity of the type II topoisomerases in DNA synthesis – bactericidal
-Active against a wide array of bacteria
-Uses: UTI, intraabdominal infections, miscellaneous infections
-Warnings: CNS (anxiety, delirium, dizziness), C. difficile infection, hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia, myasthenia gravis crisis, peripheral neuropathy,
tendon injuries (tendinitis, tendinopathy, tendon rupture), vascular (aortic aneurysm rupture)
- Should be avoided if other suitable treatment options are available

LevofloxacinBetter gram-positive activity; gram-negative activity, except Pseudomonas – respiratory
MoxifloxacinBetter gram-positive and anaerobic activity; not excreted in urine (not for UTI) – respiratory

synthesis		Macrolides
-Chemical structure: macrocyclic lactone ring attached to two sugar moieties; bind to 50S ribosomal subunit – bacteriostatic
-Uses: respiratory tract infections, STDs (chlamydia), atypical mycobacterial infections
-Macrolide resistance: ribosomal methylation or point mutations, efflux pumps, esterase drug inactivation
AzithromycinSemisynthetic macrolide
ClarithromycinSemisynthetic macrolide
ErythromycinNaturally occurring macrolide
Aminoglycosides
Gentamycin, tobramycin
-Natural antibiotics produced by soil bacteria
-Bind to 30S ribosomal subunit; cause misreading of mRNA; block formation of the 50S + 30S initiation complex and translocation – bactericidal
-Active against aerobic gram-negative bacteria; inactive against gram-positive bacteria and anaerobes
-Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity
Clindamycin
-Semi-synthetic antibiotic
-Chemical structure: amino acid linked to an amino sugar; binds to 50S ribosomal subunit – bacteriostatic
-Broad spectrum of activity against aerobic gram-positive cocci and anaerobes, including Staphylococcus and Streptococcus
- Should be avoided if other suitable treatment options are available (penicillins)
-Sometimes used as part of combination therapy for the treatment of some parasitic infections – necrotizing fasciitis
Tetracyclines
Tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline
-Chemical structure: four benzene ring structure; binds to 30S ribosomal subunit and prevent binding of incoming charged tRNA – bacteriostatic
-Only available for oral administration
-Broad spectrum of antimicrobial activity, including cell wall-deficient organisms and parasites (Plasmodia)
-Increasing resistance limits usefulness

synthesis		Sulfonamides
-Bactericidal when used in combination therapy

heading: Epidemiologic Terms
html:
• Incubation period: the time from exposure to the causative agent until the first symptoms develop (unique for each disease)
  • Infectious period / period of communicability: the time during which an infectious agent may be transferred directly or indirectly from an infected person to another; may start/stop before, during, or after symptom onset/resolution
  • Generation time: the time duration from the onset of infectiousness in a primary case to the onset of infectiousness in a secondary case infected by the primary case
  • Basic reproductive number (R): the average number of secondary infections produced by a typical case of an infection in a population where everyone is susceptible
  • o R > 1 (outbreak expected to continue; exponential growth); R < 1 (outbreak expected to end) 0 0
  • Effective reproductive number I: the average number of secondary cases per infectious case in a population made up of both susceptible and non-susceptible hosts
  • o R > 1 (number of cases will increase); R = 1 (disease is endemic); R < 1 (decline in the number of cases)
  • Antigenic drift: slow point mutations over time occurring in one virus; may result in epidemic
  • Antigenic shift: genetic elements in two viruses reassort to make a new virus/strain; may result in pandemic

heading: Vaccine Hesitancy
html:
• Vaccine hesitancy: refers to delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccine services
  • Most vaccine-hesitant parents under-immunize their children; 3% of parents are vaccine refusers

1. Pre-visit prep: collection and review of background information – immunization Hx, comorbidities, immunosuppression,

willingness to attend, identified barriers, outright trust issues, language barriers

DistrustPersonal/negative experience, mixed messages from various healthcare team members, historical context (Tuskegee)
Fear of vaccine harmVaccine produced too rapidly, trials did not include persons like them, myths on social media, limited data, needle phobia

  • Set aside extra time to counsel vaccine-hesitant parents
  • Use presumptive and motivational interviewing techniques to understand a parent’s specific vaccine concerns
  • Use simple, clear language to present evidence of disease risks and vaccine benefits/risks, fairly and accurately
  • Address pain head on
  • Community protection (herd immunity) does not guarantee personal protection

heading: Level of Disease
html:
• Sporadic: a disease that occurs infrequently and irregularly – SARS-CoV-1
  • Endemic: the constant presence of a disease in a population, and/or the typical prevalence of that disease – salmonella
  • Epidemic: increases in cases of disease above what is expected in a population – influenza in the fall and winter
  • o Outbreak is synonymous but often used for a more limited geographic area
  • Pandemic: an epidemic that has spread over several countries or continents, usually affecting many people – SARS-CoV-2

heading: Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAI)
html:
• On any given day, 1 in 31 hospital patients has at least one HAI
  • 35-55% of HAI are preventable – highest for central line associated bloodstream infections (CLABI) and catheter associated UTIs (CAUTI); lower for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and surgical site infections (SSI)
  • Each year, 8000 Canadians die from hospital-acquired infections; 220000 others get infected
  • Treatment is more costly than prevention ($129 million/year) – prolonged hospitalization, special control measures, expensive treatments (stronger antibiotics), extensive surveillance (MRSA)

heading: Sepsis
html:
• Sepsis: a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
  • Can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi
  • Sepsis is common, it is deadly, and it is an emergency – high morbidity and mortality rate (30-40%)
  • Loss of balance of proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators à cellular injury à multiple organ dysfunction (MODS)
  • The effects of inflammation are no longer localized – they are systemic
  • All organs can be involved in sepsis due to microcirculation dysfunction in the arteriolar capillary networks Cardiovascular (low BP, high HR, myocardial dysfunction), respiratory (low O, acute respiratory distress syndrome),
  • brain, coagulation system (thrombocytopenia, DIC), liver, kidneys, muscles, nerves
  • Septic shock: characterized by a low blood pressure that does not respond to fluids
  • o Blood pressure is low because blood vessels (arterioles) vasodilate, and there is a loss of intravascular fluid into the interstitial space – add vasoconstrictive agents to artificially increase BP and prevent salt-water drowning/edema
  • Therapies that have been studied and do not work: activated protein C/heparin/antithrombin III, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, nitric oxide synthesis blockade, anti-TNF antibodies/TNF receptor blocking agent, interleukin receptor antibodies, platelet activating factor (GCSF), anti-endotoxin/LPS inhibition, vitamin C and other antioxidants, immunonutrition, hemofiltration
  • It is important to recognize sepsis clinically (low temperature or fevered, tachycardia, high RR, warm/flushed, low BP), and also try to identify the cause

heading: Basic Principles of Sepsis Management
html:
Step
Early recognitionWherever you work, how ever you practice, if you see sick patients, you need a plan to NOT miss sepsis
Physiology: tachypnea/hypoxia from lung dysfunction, tachycardia/hypotension, oliguria from kidney damage
Symptomatology: rapid decline in performance status, family is concerned, major change in cognition/confusion, looks/feels very unwell
High risk factor populations: recent surgery, recent chemotherapy, immunosuppressed, elderly
Early treatmentNothing saves lives in sepsis like early, appropriate antibiotics – do whatever it takes to get the drug into the patient’s blood ASAP
From the onset of hypotension, minutes count – approximately 8% increase in mortality every hour that they are delayed
Must be broad spectrum, often multidrug therapy
Cultures are important to draw prior to antibiotic, but only if they WILL NOT DELAY ANTIBIOTIC ADMINISTRATION
Source controlPrompt identification of the source – PEx (wound, rash), imaging (CT, ultrasound)
Prompt source control – surgery, drainage, removal of infected foreign body
Life supportInvasive support for failing organs – provides time for the patient to get better (therapy, antibiotics); not fixing the problem
-Cardiovascular: vasopressors, inotropes
-Pulmonary: mechanical ventilation, prone positioning, lung protective ventilation, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)
-Renal: dialysis, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT)
-Neurologic: sedation, delirium medication

heading: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
html:
• Retrovirus that infects CD4 T cells and destroys them, resulting in a progressive loss of cell mediated immunity
  • Virus is secreted in secretions (sexual intercourse), blood (sharing needles, blood products), or transplacental transfer
text: Retrovirus that infects CD4 T cells and destroys them, resulting in a progressive loss of cell mediated immunity  Virus is secreted in secretions (sexual intercourse), blood (sharing needles, blood products), or transplacental transfer

heading: Initial infection:
html:
• HIV is taken up into cells, RNA is transcribed into DNA, gets incorporated into the host genome, viral particles are assembled
  • Mild infection symptoms 1 month after initial exposure
  • Body will form an immune response specific to HIV infection, viral load will decrease, and symptoms resolve

heading: Clinical latency:
html:
• Virus is still being replicated and destroys CD4 T cells
  • Phase lasts 8 years – patients are asymptomatic
  • Patients can live a long time symptom free, but do have other long-term health issues associated with HIV infection, such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal disease, and cancer
  • Treatment: cocktail of medications where different cellular mechanisms of viral replication are targeted

heading: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)
html:
• Patients become symptomatic with systemic symptoms and infection seen in primary immunodeficiency with T cell dysfunction
  • Weight loss, lymphadenopathy, fever
  • Opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia), malignancy (Kaposi sarcoma)
  • Phase lasts 2 years – results in death

heading: Anaphylaxis
html:
• Anaphylaxis: a serious allergic reaction with a rapid onset (minutes to within 1 hour), which may cause death
  • 0.5-5% lifetime prevalence; 1% of ER visits for acute systemic allergic reactions receive the diagnosis of anaphylaxis
  • Caused by the systemic release of mast cell and basophil mediators
  • Anaphylaxis is highly likely when any one of the following three criteria is fulfilled: 1. Sudden onset of an illness (minutes to several hours), with involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (generalized hives, itch/flush, swollen lips-tongue-uvula), and at least one of the following: a. Sudden respiratory symptoms and signs (shortness of breath, wheeze, cough, stridor, hypoxemia) b. Sudden reduced BP or symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (hypotonia/collapse, incontinence) 2. Two or more of the following that occur suddenly after exposure to a likely allergen or other trigger for that patient: a. Sudden skin or mucosal symptoms and signs (generalized hives, itch/flush, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) b. Sudden respiratory symptoms and signs (shortness of breath, wheeze, cough, stridor, hypoxemia) c. Sudden reduced BP or symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (hypotonia/collapse, incontinence) d. Sudden gastrointestinal symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, vomiting) 3. Reduced BP after exposure to a known allergen for that patient: a. Infants and children: low systolic BP (age-specific) or greater than 30% decrease in systolic BP b. Adults: systolic BP of less than 90 mm Hg or greater than 30% decrease from that person’s baseline
  • Treatment: remove the trigger, prompt administration of IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 solution, max dose = 0.3 mg), repeat epinephrine every 5-15 mins PRN, other drugs after epinephrine (O, fluids, antihistamine, salbutamol, corticosteroids)
  • Mean time to cardiorespiratory arrest: iatrogenic = 5 mins, insect sting = 15 mins, food = 30 mins

heading: Allergy Testing
html:
• Allergy testing plays a role in the diagnosis of Type I hypersensitivity reactions
  • The best allergy testing tool is the clinical Hx
  • Allergy testing sensitivity and specificity are different depending on what is being tested for and the type of testing done
  • Interpreting a test depends on the pre-/post-test probabilities and likelihood ratios, in the context of the clinical Hx
  • Pre-test probability: the clinical impression on the chance that the patient has a certain diagnosis
  • o Clinical experience, epidemiology, co-morbid conditions, risk factors, PEx findings
  • Likelihood ratio (LR): the likelihood that a given test result would be expected in a patient with the target disorder compared to the likelihood that that same result would be expected in a patient without the target disorder
  • o Positive LR: the odds that a person who has what you are looking for has a positive test compared to a person who does not have what you are looking for but has a positive test; Sn/(1-Sp)
  • o Negative LR: the odds that a person who has what you are looking for has a negative test compared to a person who does not have what you are looking for but has a negative test; (1-Sn)/Sp
  • o Calculate from sensitivity and specificity or use a nomogram
  • Cross reactivity: can occur when there is ~70% homology between antigens such that the tertiary structure is conserved
  • o Patients with food pollen syndrome to birch can get oral pruritis to almond
  • Food allergen proteins used for skin prick testing and serum IgE testing are commercially prepared Purified food protein – should contain all relevant allergens; amount of each allergen is variable with each batch
  • o Recombinant extract – known allergens are made using bacteria vectors; often contains the major known allergens, but will not contain allergens that are not well known (false negative results); can be used to spike purified food protein extracts for clinically important allergens that are at low concentration
  • Environmental allergen proteins: dust mites (feces), cat/dog (dander), seasonal allergens (pollen), mold (spores)

Isolate the patient’s serum and add it to the protein; wash away the serum, leaving behind the bound IgE 4. Add a marker to measure the IgE bound; measure how much IgE is bound

  • in pregnant patients, beta blockers can interfere with allergic reaction treatments, do the challenge in hospital and consider an IV prior to the challenge

heading: Autoimmune Disease
html:
• Immune tolerance: antigen-specific immunological unresponsiveness to self-antigens
  • o Central tolerance: immature self-reactive lymphocytes are negatively selected/deleted in the BM and thymus gland
  • o Lymphocytes that have low affinity receptors for self-antigen will enter the periphery
  • o Peripheral tolerance: mature self-reactive lymphocytes are addressed by the spleen and lymph nodes through immunologic ignorance (anatomical barrier), anergy/inhibition (blocks CD28:CD80), deletion (Fas ligand), and suppression (regulatory T cells – IL-10, TGF- β)
  • Autoimmunity: failure of the immune system to recognize self-cells, and the resultant destruction of these self-cells

heading: Pathology of Chronic Inflammation
html:
• Chronic inflammation: inflammation that has been present for weeks or months
  • It is usually accompanied by attempts at tissue repair
  • Potential causes: persistent infection / injury (TB), hypersensitivity (rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, IBD), chronic exposure to toxins (silicosis, atherosclerosis)

heading: Granulomas
html:
• Granuloma: an aggregation of macrophages surrounded by T lymphocytes that forms in response to chronic inflammation
  • The activated macrophages tend to accumulate cytoplasm and are called epithelioid histiocytes because of their resemblance to epithelial cells
  • o Sometimes their nuclei resemble footprints in the sand Sometimes many macrophages fuse to form multinucleate giant cells (Langhan’s cells)
  • Granulomas are often an attempt to contain something that is difficult to eradicate – talc in IV drug use, sutures
  • White nodule with a chalky/cheesy center – necrotising/caseating as a result of hypoxia and free radical injury
  • Common sites: lungs, lymph nodes, GI tract
  • Potential causes: mycobacterial (TB), fungal (histoplasmosis), bacterial (cat scratch disease); sarcoidosis, vasculitis, Chron’s disease, foreign body reaction, malignancy
  • Make sure the patient does not have TB before starting an immunosuppressive treatment for a non-infectious condition

heading: Approach to Fever in the Immunocompromised Host
html:
• Different clinical conditions can impair different aspects of the immune system, which predisposes to different infections Diabetes mellitus: low C4; decreased cytokine response after stimulation, chemotaxis, killing, and phagocytosis
  • o Renal failure: uremia is associated with defective co-stimulatory function of antigen-presenting cells (hypothesized to contribute to poor response to vaccines (Hepatitis B); decreased lymphocyte numbers in dialysis patients
  • Immune deficiency can be a very dynamic process – it is all about timing
  • o HIV risk: CD4 < 50 (M. avium, CMV retinitis, lymphomas), CD4 > 500 (similar infections as non-infected individuals, TB)
  • o High risk of invasive mold infections: chronic granulomatous disease, allogenic HSCT, lung/heart transplant, AML/MDS
  • o Allogeneic stem cell transplant: patient receives healthy stem cells from a donor to replace their own stem cells that have been conditioned by treatment with radiation or high doses of chemotherapy § Pre-engraftment (neutropenia), post-engraftment (NK cells recover), late phase (CD4 T cells recover)
  • May not see fevers with cytokine-blocking medications: anakinra, rilonacept, tocilizumab, infliximab, golimumab, adalimumab
  • When developing the DDx, think of the patient’s immune status – use the same differential + opportunistic infections + context
  • o Presentation is commonly different between immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients
  • Vaccination is imperative in immunocompromised patients
  • o Live virus vaccines are generally unsafe
  • o Give vaccines before immunosuppressive medications when possible
  • Give an antimicrobial prophylaxis drug to patients with HIV or transplant recipients for infections that do not have a vaccine
